The control is invisible until an auditor or incident asks for it, so it is routinely deferred. This gate exists because the deployment schema advertised an "audit logging gate" for containsPii environments while no such gate was wired.

gates.title: Content-Security-Policy Set on Externally-Accessible Services
gates.description: Any environment reachable from the public internet must serve a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header that is not wide-open. A missing or `default-src *` / `unsafe-inline` CSP provides no XSS mitigation. The policy must at minimum constrain default-src and script-src to known origins.
gates.check: Confirm a Content-Security-Policy response header exists and is restrictive on every environment declared externallyAccessible: true. Reject a policy that is absent, set to `default-src *`, or relies on `unsafe-inline`/`unsafe-eval` for script-src without a nonce/hash. Live check: curl -sI "$API_URL" | grep -i 'content-security-policy'
gates.passCriterion: A Content-Security-Policy header is present and constrains at least default-src and script-src to explicit origins (no bare wildcard, no unguarded unsafe-inline) for every externally-accessible environment.
gates.failureMessage: Externally-accessible environment has no Content-Security-Policy, or a policy permissive enough to provide no XSS protection (wildcard default-src or unguarded unsafe-inline).
gates.fixHint: Set a restrictive CSP via middleware (helmet contentSecurityPolicy) or proxy. Start from default-src 'self' and widen deliberately per asset origin.
gates.evidence: CSP is the most effective defense-in-depth control against reflected and stored XSS, but is frequently shipped either absent or as an ineffective wildcard because a permissive policy "works" in the browser without warning. This gate exists because the deployment schema advertised a "CSP gate" for externallyAccessible environments while no such gate was wired.

gates.title: PII Masked in Logs for PII-Bearing Environments
gates.description: In any environment that can hold real personally identifiable information, application logs must not emit raw PII (email, full name, phone, national id, card number, password, token). Sensitive fields must be masked, redacted, or omitted at the logging boundary. Raw PII in logs is the most common way regulated data leaks into systems with weaker access controls (log aggregators, error trackers, terminals).
gates.check: Scan source for logging calls that pass known-sensitive fields directly. Grep for logger/console/print statements that interpolate fields named password, token, secret, ssn, creditCard, cardNumber, email, phone without a mask/redact wrapper. Example: grep -rEn '(log(ger)?\.(info|debug|warn|error)|console\.(log|info)|print)\(.*(password|token|secret|ssn|card|creditCard)' src/ Each hit must route the value through a masking helper (e.g. mask(), redact()).
gates.passCriterion: No logging statement emits a raw sensitive field. Sensitive values are masked or omitted before reaching any log sink in PII-bearing environments.
gates.failureMessage: A logging statement appears to emit raw PII/secret in an environment marked containsPii: true. Route the value through a masking/redaction helper or omit it.
gates.fixHint: Wrap sensitive values in a mask()/redact() helper before logging, or configure a log processor that strips known sensitive keys.
gates.evidence: PII in plaintext logs is a top cause of reportable data exposure: the data is copied to log aggregators and error trackers that have broader access than the primary datastore, defeating the database-level controls. Masking at the log boundary is standard (OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet) but easy to forget on a new log line. This gate exists because the deployment schema advertised a "PII logging gate" / "data masking gate" for containsPii environments while no such gate was wired.

gates.title: Security Headers Present on Externally-Accessible Services
gates.description: Any environment reachable from the public internet must serve the baseline HTTP security headers: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), X-Content-Type-Options (nosniff), X-Frame-Options (or frame-ancestors via CSP), and Referrer-Policy. Missing headers leave externally-facing services open to clickjacking, MIME sniffing, protocol downgrade, and referrer leakage.
gates.check: Inspect the server/middleware configuration (e.g. helmet for Express, secure headers middleware for FastAPI/Django, the reverse-proxy config, or a live curl -I against the deployed URL) and confirm these response headers are set: Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options (or a CSP frame-ancestors directive), Referrer-Policy. For a deployed target: curl -sI "$API_URL" | grep -iE 'strict-transport-security|x-content-type-options|x-frame-options|referrer-policy'
gates.passCriterion: All four baseline security headers are present in responses from every environment declared externallyAccessible: true (verified in middleware config or against the live endpoint).
gates.failureMessage: Externally-accessible environment is missing one or more baseline security headers (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy). Add a security-headers middleware (helmet, secure, etc.).
gates.fixHint: Add a security-headers middleware (Express: helmet(); FastAPI: secure.Secure; Django: SecurityMiddleware) or set the headers at the reverse proxy.
gates.evidence: Public services shipped without HSTS or X-Frame-Options are a recurring source of clickjacking and SSL-strip incidents. The headers are cheap, static, and universally recommended (OWASP Secure Headers Project), yet routinely omitted because nothing fails without them — exactly the silent gap a gate closes. This gate exists because the deployment schema advertised "security headers gate" for externallyAccessible environments while no such gate was wired.

gates.title: External-Render Templates Require a Snapshot Test
gates.description: Any template that renders content consumed outside the app — PDF, email, CSV/JSON export, public webhook payload — must have a snapshot test that freezes a fixture input and compares the rendered output. Visual code review does not catch label drift, raw-enum leaks, or layout breaks. Snapshot diffs require explicit human approval; CI must not auto-update them.
gates.check: 1. Identify modules that render external output (pdf, email, export, template, report renderers). 2. Confirm each has a colocated snapshot test that renders a fixture and asserts against a stored snapshot. 3. Confirm CI runs snapshots in non-updating mode (no --updateSnapshot / -u in the pipeline).
gates.passCriterion: Every external-render template has a snapshot test over a fixture; CI fails on snapshot drift rather than silently rewriting it.
gates.evidence: Vairix DELTA-058 — the generated PDF rendered raw enum values (strongly_recommended, quick_win) in user-visible badges for roughly three weeks. tsc passed, units passed, no test exercised the rendered HTML. A single snapshot test of the template would have failed the moment the label leaked.

provenance.finding: DELTA-058 — PDF leaked raw enum labels for ~3 weeks; no test rendered the template output

gates.title: LLM-Output-Consuming Code Must Test Against Recorded Replay Fixtures
gates.description: Any code that consumes model output — directly from an LLM client or downstream of a generation pipeline — must have at least one test that runs against a real recorded output (a replay fixture), not only hand-rolled synthetic mocks. Synthetic mocks encode the shape the author imagined; production emits enum values, escape sequences, and orderings the author did not. Capture real outputs with metadata (model, timestamp, phase) and replay them.
gates.check: 1. Identify spec files for handlers under ai/ or pipeline/ (LLM consumers). 2. Confirm each imports at least one replay fixture from a recorded-outputs corpus. 3. Synthetic mocks are allowed only as a complement, never the sole input. 4. New pipeline phases add a fixture before their first green commit.
gates.passCriterion: Every LLM-output-consuming test exercises at least one recorded replay fixture; no model-consumer is tested on synthetic mocks alone.
gates.evidence: Vairix DELTA-088 — the promote-pattern endpoint tested with severity "high" but the model emitted "moderate"/"severe", breaking the enum cast with a 500 in production. DELTA-051/079 — the model emitted double-escaped JSON the synthetic mocks never produced. Tests mocked the OpenAI client, so the real output shape never reached an assertion.

provenance.finding: DELTA-088 — endpoint 500 on real LLM enum value never present in synthetic test mocks

gates.title: Bug Fix Requires a Regression Test That Fails Before the Fix
gates.description: Every fix that closes a reported bug must add a regression test exercising the concrete input that broke (payload, document, click sequence, model output), and that test must fail against the pre-fix code. The breaking input becomes a permanent fixture. Without this, the same failure class returns with a near-identical sample because the lesson lived only in a changelog, not in an executable check.
gates.check: 1. Detect commits whose type is fix( and whose message or linked tracker marks a bug transitioning to resolved. 2. Confirm the same commit adds or modifies a test under a regression fixtures path. 3. Confirm the test encodes the actual breaking input, not a synthetic restatement. 4. Ideally confirm the test fails against the parent commit.
gates.passCriterion: Every bug-closing fix commit touches a regression test/fixture that reproduces the original breaking input and would fail before the fix.
gates.evidence: Vairix DELTA-079 was a regression of DELTA-051, itself a regression of DELTA-007 — a JSON-escape sanitizer bug returning under a cousin sample each time. The lesson was captured in a Corrections Log but the breaking document never entered fixtures, so the same class broke three times.

provenance.finding: DELTA-079/051/007 — same sanitizer bug class recurred three times; breaking sample never captured as a fixture

gates.title: React — All Components Have TypeScript Props Types (No Implicit Any)
gates.description: Every React component must have an explicit TypeScript props interface or type alias. Implicit `any` props types defeat TypeScript's ability to catch breaking prop changes at compile time — a prop renamed in a parent breaks at runtime, not at build time. This gate enforces the baseline type safety that makes component refactoring safe.
gates.check:
Set `strict: true` in tsconfig.json (activates noImplicitAny). Confirm with: npx tsc --noEmit (must exit 0). Add to .eslintrc: "@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any": "error" to prevent `any` workarounds. For React props specifically: every function component must have either:
  - An explicit interface: `interface Props { ... }; const MyComp = (props: Props) => ...`
  - An inline type: `const MyComp = ({ name }: { name: string }) => ...`
Components that accept children must type them: `children: React.ReactNode`.
gates.passCriterion: `npx tsc --noEmit` exits 0 with `strict: true` enabled. Zero @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any violations in src/**/*.tsx. All component props interfaces are explicitly declared.
gates.evidence: Components without typed props are the #1 source of breaking changes invisible at compile time in React codebases. TypeScript strict mode is zero-cost to add at project setup and exponentially expensive to retrofit into existing code. Adding it as a gate at project initialization costs nothing and prevents an entire class of runtime regressions from ever entering the codebase.

gates.title: Dependency CVE Audit — Pre-Commit Blocking Gate
gates.description: Audit all project dependencies for known CVEs before every commit. Block on HIGH or CRITICAL vulnerabilities in direct dependencies.
gates.check: Run the project's ecosystem audit tool before every commit. Block on HIGH or CRITICAL CVEs in direct dependencies. See tools-registry.yaml for ecosystem-specific commands: - Node.js: npm audit --audit-level=high - Python: pip-audit --severity high - Rust: cargo audit --deny warnings - Go: govulncheck ./... - Java: dependency-check --failBuildOnCVSS 7
gates.passCriterion: Zero HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs in direct dependencies. All transitive CVEs triaged with documented disposition (accepted, remediated, or suppressed with reason).
gates.evidence: The bcrypt -> @mapbox/node-pre-gyp -> tar CVE chain is a well-known example where a conceptually dev-only dependency introduced a production CVE. Pre-commit audit would have caught this at install time. Supply chain attacks via transitive dependencies are the fastest-growing vulnerability class as of 2025.

gates.title: Mutation Testing Gate — Pre-Release Test Quality Verification
gates.description: Verify that the test suite actually catches real bugs by injecting synthetic faults into the codebase and confirming that tests fail when the code is broken.
gates.check: Run mutation testing on changed files. Inject synthetic bugs: operator replacement (== to !=, + to -, < to <=), boundary inversion (off-by-one), and return value mutation (return null, return empty). If tests don't catch the injected bug, the test suite is checking the wrong things. Minimum score 80% on changed files. Tools: Stryker (JS/TS), PITest (Java), mutmut (Python), cargo-mutants (Rust).
gates.passCriterion: MSI >= 80% on changed files. No surviving mutants in critical path code (auth, permissions, financial calculations).
gates.evidence: GS experiments found 40-50% MSI on naive agent-generated test suites. Between 1-2 out of 3 agent-generated tests provide no real coverage. Explicit mutation gate consistently raises this to 80%+.

gates.title: OWASP ASVS Level 1 — Static Security Analysis at Commit Time
gates.description: Run static security checks on every commit to catch the most common vulnerability classes before they reach code review.
gates.check: Run a static security analyzer appropriate for the project's language. Checks must cover: (1) hardcoded secrets and credentials, (2) SQL/command injection patterns via string concatenation, (3) eval() with dynamic input, (4) dependency CVEs. See tools-registry.yaml for language-specific tools. These are LEVEL 1 checks: they run at every commit with no human review required.
gates.passCriterion: Zero HIGH/CRITICAL findings from static analyzer. All pre-commit hooks exit 0.
gates.evidence: Static analysis at commit time catches ~70% of OWASP Top 10 issues before they reach code review. SQL injection and hardcoded credential patterns are reliably detected statically without running the application.

gates.title: Playwright UI Smoke Test — Live Page Verification with Screenshot
gates.description: After every deploy or significant UI change, navigate to the live URL with Playwright, wait for all async data to load, assert that critical elements are present and non-empty, and save a full-page screenshot as a proof artifact. This catches an entire class of bugs that unit and API tests cannot see: blank pages, broken async fetches, CSS layout collapses, missing data sections, and rendering errors that only appear in a real browser against real infrastructure.
gates.check:
Write a Playwright script (scripts/smoke-test.js or tests/smoke/ui.spec.ts) that: 1. Navigates to the live URL with { waitUntil: "networkidle" } 2. Waits for async data to resolve (waitForFunction on a data-populated element) 3. Asserts critical elements: page title/heading, primary data section populated,
   no error messages visible (target specific error elements, not body.textContent
   which includes script source), navigation present
4. Takes a full-page screenshot and saves it as an artifact 5. Exits with code 1 on any assertion failure Run against staging before promotion, and against production within 5 minutes of deploy. Add to CI as a post-deploy step. Tool: Playwright (playwright.dev) — language-agnostic, works with any web UI.
gates.passCriterion: All element assertions pass. Screenshot artifact saved and visually confirms the page renders correctly. Script exits 0. Total run time < 60 seconds. No blank sections, no error messages, no spinner/loading states still active after the wait-for-data step.
gates.evidence: First run on genspec-portal caught two bugs invisible to unit tests: (1) Gates with multiple tags rendered once per tag — the page was visually cluttered with duplicates. Zero unit tests would catch this; it requires seeing the rendered output. (2) A naive body.textContent error check matched the JS source code string 'Failed to load taxonomy.json' — triggering a false positive that masked the real check. Both bugs found and fixed before any user saw the page. Pattern holds: the gap between "tests pass" and "page works" is exactly what Playwright closes.

gates.title: UX Pattern Docs — Required Before Common Interactions
gates.description: Require docs/patterns/ with at minimum error.md and loading.md before page, modal, or table components are committed. These pattern docs are the single source of truth that prevents each feature team from implementing error and loading states differently. Without them, AI-assisted development generates fresh UI patterns per session.
gates.check: When staged files include any file matching *page*, *Page*, *screen*, *Screen*, *modal*, *Modal*, *table*, or *Table* naming patterns, verify that docs/patterns/error.md and docs/patterns/loading.md exist. If either is missing, block the commit.
gates.passCriterion: docs/patterns/ contains at minimum error.md and loading.md before any page, modal, or table components are committed. Each pattern doc defines: when to use, appearance, component API, error cases, and empty state behaviour.
gates.failureMessage: UX pattern docs missing. Create docs/patterns/error.md and docs/patterns/loading.md before implementing page or interactive components.
gates.fixHint: mkdir -p docs/patterns && touch docs/patterns/error.md docs/patterns/loading.md docs/patterns/empty.md docs/patterns/modals.md docs/patterns/tables.md
gates.evidence: Applications without shared UX pattern docs develop inconsistent error, loading, and empty state treatments across features. Users encounter different behaviours for the same interaction type in different parts of the same app — a trust-eroding inconsistency that emerges specifically from AI-assisted development where each session starts fresh without context from prior implementation decisions.
